primary_claim: In an initial GridWorld goal-directedness testbed built for a new behavioural-plus-probing measurement framework (Project Telos), gpt-oss-20B's elicited navigation policies frequently deviate from the optimal policy through recurring error patterns (e.g. action cycles between two squares, moves directly into walls) observed across many grids and trials.
contradicts_or_qualifies: Draws on but diverges from inverse reinforcement learning, which requires a strong rationality assumption; this project targets the broader category of 'goals' rather than reward functions to avoid that limitation
stated_future_work: Move from GridWorld to more realistic, high-stakes environments such as cybersecurity tasks or dangerous capability testing, to study sandbagging or scheming as testable hypotheses
Extend goal-directedness evaluations to more complex LLM behaviours and goal structures
Publish a future post diving deeper into the philosophical/psychological/economic literature underpinning the framework
limitations_stated: The project is in its very early stages (six weeks in) and results so far are preliminary
Current experiments are limited to a fully observable, memoryless agent setting where the policy at each square is solicited independently of trajectory
It remains unclear how close to an optimal policy an agent needs to be to qualify as 'goal-directed', and whether confounding biases (e.g. directional preferences) explain observed errors
quote: Fig. 1b (middle) shows a case in which the optimal action is reversed over two squares. If the agent followed this policy, it would move infinitely between squares r4c4 and r5c4, never reaching the goal.
